candidates.description_summary: Terraced two-bay three-storey house over raised basement. Flemish-bond red brick, granite plinth, slate roof behind parapet, gauged-brick window openings and two-over-two timber sliding sash windows. The entrance has an Ionic doorcase, original timber door and fanlight; a shared granite platform and steps serve the frontage.
candidates.appraisal_summary: NIAH describes the house as one of a terrace of five dating from the early nineteenth century, built during city expansion associated with the North Circular Road and railway. It retains its original door and doorcase, façade composition and ironmongery despite upper-floor wall rebuilding.

candidates.official_title: Parcels Post office, 102–106 Amiens Street, Preston Street, Dublin 1, DUBLIN
candidates.address: 102–106 Amiens Street / Preston Street, Dublin 1, Ireland
candidates.description_summary: Detached seven-bay two-storey former railway parcels office over raised basement, with a Dutch-gable-fronted return and rear extension. Decorative Flemish Revival red-brick elevations, shaped gables, limestone copings, engaged pilasters, elaborate chimneystack, moulded cornices and a detailed entrance with spoked fanlight.
candidates.appraisal_summary: NIAH identifies the building as designed by J. Howard Pentland in 1892 as part of the Great Northern Railway Terminus complex. Its scale, decorative Flemish Revival detailing and former role in railway mail handling contribute to its architectural and historical interest.

candidates.official_title: Hugh Ward & Co. Solicitors, 9 Seville Place, Dublin 1, DUBLIN
candidates.description_summary: End-of-terrace two-bay two-storey house over raised basement, now in office use. Yellow Flemish-bond brick walls on granite plinth, M-profile slate roof, gauged-brick window openings, granite platform and ten granite steps, moulded entrance surround, Doric doorcase and decorative cast-iron railings.
candidates.appraisal_summary: NIAH describes the building as formerly mid-terrace and now terminating a terrace of seven houses at its southern end. Renovation removed some external detail, but the Victorian façade contributes to the residential streetscape and continues the traditional scale of the opposite late-Georgian terrace.
